question: A 50-year-old woman comes to the physician because of intermittent pain and numbness in her right hand for 6 weeks. She has a pins-and-needles sensation that worsens at night and is relieved when she shakes her hand. She also has episodic left knee pain throughout the day. She has a history of hypertension controlled with lisinopril. She takes over-the-counter medications for constipation. Her BMI is 35 kg/m2. Her mother has a history of rheumatoid arthritis. She looks fatigued. Her pulse is 57/min and blood pressure is 120/75 mm Hg. On physical examination, there is normal range of motion in the wrists and digits. Sensation is decreased to light touch in the thumb and index finger. There is no thenar muscle atrophy. Deep tendon reflexes are 1+ and there is mild edema in the legs. Which of the following treatments is most likely to benefit the patient?

enhanced_information: The patient's symptoms of intermittent pain and numbness in the right hand, particularly worsening at night and relieved by shaking, are indicative of carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS). The decreased sensation in the thumb and index finger supports this diagnosis, and the absence of thenar muscle atrophy suggests that the condition is not yet severe. Mild edema in the legs may be unrelated to the hand symptoms. Conservative treatment options for CTS typically include NSAIDs like ibuprofen for pain relief. Surgical decompression is considered if conservative measures fail, but it is not the first-line treatment. Methotrexate and oral prednisone are not appropriate as there are no systemic inflammatory signs or indications of rheumatoid arthritis affecting the current symptoms. Therefore, ibuprofen is the most likely treatment to benefit the patient at this stage.
